editorial_checks: Two full real-case essays, not fictional scenes or a compressed abstract of the papers. English independently written; Traditional Chinese carries complete prose. No front-end DD or proposition labels.

Steward's announced September 2016 agreements and 3 October closing are distinct. The approximately $1.25 billion package is five property purchases for leaseback, four first-mortgage loans and preferred investment, not the purchase of nine hospitals' real estate or a measure of spending on patients.
The 4.9% economic interest is not management control. General financing constraints are explained as analytical possibilities, not as evidence that the landlord directed clinical decisions.

The 2010 attorney general's contemporaneous assessment of capital needs, alternatives and public interest is retained. It is neither proof that refusing the acquisition would have been worse nor approval of every subsequent transaction. Monitoring commitments are not a performance audit.

The hospital narrative stops at 6 May 2024. The state's dated operating statement does not promise later continuity. Its criticism is attributed, not converted into a court finding. Care continuity and protection of a particular incumbent are distinguished.

No dividends, expansion expenditure, individual injury or full bankruptcy causation are inferred from transaction totals. The eight-year gap requires further operating and financial evidence; different owners, lenders, managers and dates are not collapsed into a single actor.

The ratings essay follows S&P's agreed facts: 7 February surveillance recommendations and 12 February committee action. Approximately 30/20 transactions are distinguished from 18 tranches across 11 transactions. Internal watch, public negative watch and downgrade remain distinct.

The 10 July 2007 watch action on 612 classes is distinguished from 12 July downgrades. The CDO discussion concerns unchanged existing criteria for anticipated negative RMBS actions, not an invented claim that no ratings ever changed.

The $1.375 billion settlement's date and parties, agreed facts, congressional investigation and Justice Department characterizations are differentiated. No criminal conviction, admission by another rating agency or sole-cause explanation of the crisis is invented.

Regulatory and institutional reliance is bounded, not a claim that all funds had to buy AAA or all holders were forced to sell. Ratings' credit-risk scope is distinguished from price, liquidity and a universal investment recommendation.

Conflicts identify questions for evidence, not proof that every rating is manipulated. Deliberation is not automatically concealment. Subscriber payment, competition, expert review and public/nonprofit ownership are not presented as automatic cures.

Earlier article bodies and publication receipts remain unchanged. Navigation and the series landing expand without adding a new library category. Future cases remain open, not represented as published.
